title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.3 Friedenwald’s equation of ocular rigidity
The original Freidenwald’s equation of ocular rigidity assumes that: \[
\frac{\partial P}{\partial V} = K \cdot P \Leftrightarrow P = P_0 e^{K \cdot V}
\] We estimate the ocular rigidity \(K\) using two measurements of intraocular pressure \(P_1\) and \(P_2\) and the corresponding ocular volumes \(V_1\) and \(V_2\): \[
K = \log \left( \frac{P_2}{P_1} \right) / (V_2 - V_1)
\tag{1.1}\]
We estimate \(V_2\) and \(V_1\) using \(CT\) and \(\Delta CT\) where \(CT\) is the choroidal thickness and \(\Delta CT\) is the change in choroidal thickness between two measurements. \(P_2\) and \(P_1\) are the intraocular pressures at the two measurements. Let’s note the axial length \(\alpha\). It is the distance from the corneal surface to an interference peak corresponding to the RPE. We introduce a the corrected axial length \(\hat{\alpha} = 0.83 \alpha\). The spherical radius during diastole and (end of) systole are estimated as: \[
r_1 = \frac{\hat{\alpha}}{2} + CT
\] and \[
r_2 = \frac{\hat{\alpha}}{2} + CT + \Delta CT
\] From which we estimate the change in ocular volume \(\Delta V\) as: \[
\Delta V = \frac{4}{3} \pi (r_2^3 - r_1^3)
\] In practise, we also introduce a correction factor \(c\) to account for the fact that the eye is not a perfect sphere. The corrected change in ocular volume is then: \[
\Delta V_{corr} = c \Delta V \] with \(c = 2/3\).

1.4 Visual field characteristics
The Humphrey Visual Field (HVF) is a common test to assess the visual field of patients.






Note



Taken from https://eyerounds.org/tutorials/VF-testing/#gsc.tab=0 During Humphrey Visual Field (HVF) testing, the patient places his head in the chinrest and fixes his gaze toward a central fixation point in a large, white bowl. […] It assesses the ability to see a non-mobile stimulus which remains for a brief moment (200 ms) in the visual field. When the patient sees a presented stimulus, he presses the button on a handheld remote control. Different locations within a given region of the visual field are tested until the threshold, or the stimulus intensity seen 50% of the time, is seen at each test location.


The HVF test provides several metrics, including the mean deviation (MD), pattern standard deviation (PSD), and visual field index (VFI). Yaqub (2012) is a good reference on how to interpret these values. In short: MD is a measure of the overall deviation of the visual field from normal, PSD measures localized irregularities in the visual field, and VFI is a summary measure of the overall visual field status. In even shorter: the lower the MD, the worse the visual field. The higher the PSD, the worse the visual field. The lower the VFI, the worse the visual field.




Yaqub, Moustafa. 2012. “Visual Fields Interpretation in Glaucoma: A Focus on Static Automated Perimetry.” Community Eye Health 25 (79-80): 1–8.

title: 2  Review of the Literature
text:
2.0.1 Miscellaneous

Abe et al. (2015) offer an interesting description of the role of the lamina cribrosa in the pathophysiology of glaucoma. The lamina cribrosa is a sieve-like structure that allows the passage of retinal ganglion cell axons from the eye to the brain. It is composed of connective tissue and is supported by the sclera. The lamina cribrosa is also a site of mechanical stress, as it is subjected to intraocular pressure and cerebrospinal fluid pressure. It has been suggested that the lamina cribrosa may be a site of axonal injury in glaucoma, and that changes in it may be an early indicator of glaucomatous damage. Specifically, a thinner LC is associated with glaucomatous damages. They suggest a very interesting hypothesis: glaucoma is caused by the trans-laminar pressure gradient (i.e. the difference between IOP and cerebrospinal fluid pressure). The hypothesis is supported by the work of Ren et al. (2010): a low cerebrospinal fluid pressure (CSF-P) is associated with open-angle glaucoma in eyes with normal intraocular pressure (IOP).







Conclusion from Ren et al. (2010)



In open-angle glaucoma with normal IOP, cerebrospinal fluid pressure (CSF-P) is abnormally low, leading to an abnormally high trans-lamina cribrosa pressure difference. Pathogenetically, a low CSF-P in normal-IOP glaucoma may be similar to a high IOP in high-IOP glaucoma. Consequently, the glaucomatous visual field defect is positively correlated with the trans-lamina cribrosa pressure difference and inversely correlated with the CSF-P. In nonglaucomatous subjects, CSF-P, blood pressure, and IOP are significantly associated with each other








More about CSF-P





Jonas et al. (2015) offer an interesting review on the CSF-P and its role with the physiology of the eye. - Thicker subfoveal choroidal thickness was associated with higher estimated CSFP. - Larger retinal vein diameters and higher vein-to-artery diameter ratios were significantly associated with higher estimated CSFP (P = 0.001). In contrast, retinal arterial diameters were not significantly associated with estimated CSFP nor were other microvascular abnormalities such as arteriovenous crossing signs. In a reverse manner, higher estimated CSFP was correlated with wider retinal veins and higher vein-to-artery diameter ratio, but not with retinal artery diameters or other retinal microvascular abnormalities.




Werff (1981) suggests to use another metric to estimate the rigidity: \[
\Delta V = \frac{1}{K} (P_2^{1/3} - P_1^{1/3})
\] where \(\Delta V\) is the change in volume and \(P_2\) and \(P_1\) are the intraocular pressures at the two measurements. Other definitions are also listed in section Section 2.0.6 and Section 2.0.7.



2.0.2 Structural Measurements for Monitoring Change in Glaucoma: Comparing Retinal Nerve Fiber Layer Thickness With Minimum Rim Width and Area
Structural measurements are noisy. Gardiner et al. (2015) propose to use the LSNR (Longitudinal Signal-to-Noise Ratio). Instead of comparing the slope of a structural measurement over time, they propose to compare the slope divided by the standard deviation of the residuals. This is a measure of how much signal there is in the noise. The more negative the LSNR, the more likely it is that the slope is real and not just noise. They compare three structural measurements: the retinal nerve fiber layer thickness (RNFLT), the minimum rim width (MRW) and the minimum rim area (MRA). They find that the RNFLT has a better LSNR than MRW or MRA. Although MRW and MRA may be more sensitive for early detection of glaucomatous damage, these data suggest that RNFLT may be preferable for monitoring change. Cohort: 157 eyes of 157 participants with high-risk ocular hypertension or non–end-stage glaucoma (mean deviation [MD] from −22 to +3 dB). Participants were tested approximately every 6 months for at least six visits.











2.0.3 Clinical Utility of Bruch Membrane Opening-Minimum Rim Width for Detecting Early Glaucoma in Myopic Eyes
Park et al. (2021) conduct a study to determine the diagnostic value of BMO-MRW compared with peripapillary retinal nerve fiber layer (pRNFL) thickness for detecting early glaucoma in patients with moderate to severe myopia. Global analyses for the discrimination of early glaucoma in all myopic subjects showed comparable AUCs between BMO-MRW and pRNFL thickness [AUC 0.952 (95% confidence interval, 0.918-0.975) and 0.934 (95% confidence interval, 0.896-0.961), respectively, P=0.345]. However, in sectoral analysis, BMO-MRW showed significantly better diagnostic performance than pRNFL thickness except for the superotemporal sector.











2.0.4 The Association Between Ocular Rigidity and Neuroretinal Damage in Glaucoma
Sayah et al. (2020) aims to evaluate the relationship between OR and neuroretinal damage caused by glaucoma. Significant positive correlations were found between OR and minimum GCC thickness (r = 0.325, P = 0.001), average GCC thickness (r = 0.320, P = 0.002), rim area (r = 0.344, P < 0.001), and RNFL thickness in the superior (r = 0.225, P = 0.023), and inferior (r = 0.281, P = 0.004) quadrants. These correlations were generally greater than those found for CCT, CH, and CRF. Furthermore, no correlation was found between OR and corneal biomechanical parameters. Cohort: 108 subjects (22 healthy, 23 suspected glaucoma, and 63 glaucoma (early to advance)). The main results are sumarized in Figure 2.1, which represents the partial correlation between OR and neuroretinal damage, adjusted for age, sex, and axial length.








Figure 2.1







2.0.5 Association between ocular biometric parameters and scleral rigidity as measured by fundus pulsation optical coherence elastography in eyes with and without glaucoma
Bojikian et al. (2026) published a study to evaluate the association between ocular biometric parameters and scleral rigidity as measured by fundus pulsation optical coherence elastography (FP-OCE) in eyes with and without glaucoma. The study included 58 eyes with glaucoma and 36 control eyes. In Figure 2.2, we see the choroidal max strain in glaucoma vs normal eyes they obtain. In short, higher maximum choroidal strain (which is either a more pulsatile choroid or a thinner choroid) is midly associated with glaucoma, which in turns indicate that a lower ocular rigidity is associated with glaucoma.








Figure 2.2







2.0.6 Non-invasive Clinical Measurement of Ocular Rigidity and Comparison to Biomechanical and Morphological Parameters in Glaucomatous and Healthy Subjects
Ma, Moroi, and Roberts (2021) offer almost the same methodology as we do in this study, to ONH videos. They show that there is a stronger correlation between ocular rigidity and sclearal stiffness (R=0.62, measured using the stiffness parameter at the highest concavity [SP-HC]) vs corneal stiffness (stiffness parameter at the first applanation [SP-A1], R=0.41). There is a positive corelation with the static pressure-volume ratio (P/V, R=0.72). They do the same linearization of \(\Delta V \approx 4\pi R^2\Delta CT\). They define \(R\) as half the axial length.
The coneaosclera properties were measured using with a Corvis ST, a non contact tonometer coupled with a high-speed Scheimpflug camera. The corneal stiffness was measured using the stiffness parameter at the first applanation (SP-A1). The scleral stiffness was measured using the stiffness parameter at the highest concavity (SP-HC). The results (figure Figure 2.3) they obntain are not significant due to a very small cohort (n=6 for glaucoma, n=23 for control)








Figure 2.3







2.0.7 Ocular Rigidity in Living Human Eyes
Pallikaris et al. (2005) proceed with an actual measurement of the rigidity (unfortunately, not defined as we did, i.e, they define \(K = \frac{\Delta P}{\Delta V}\) ). They inject saline in the eye by interval, until they reach an IOP of 60 mmHg or 200 μL of saline. The average \(R^2\) they obtain is 0.92 (maybe the linearization of the relation is actually a good idea; they indicate the linear relationship was the best fit they got). They also reference the work of Silver and Geyer (2000), that indicate that the best fit for the pressure-volume relationship is: \[
\Delta V = V \cdot (C+C_0\log{P} + C_1 \cdot P)
\] where \(C\), \(C_0\) and \(C_1\) are numerical constants.

3.1 Statistical tests
This chapter will focus on describing the statistical methods used in the study.

title: 3  Statistical Analysis
text:
3.1.1 Introduction
The motivation behind statistical test is to determine whether there is a significant difference between two or more groups with regards to a specific variable.
The idea is to formulate a null hypothesis \(H_0\) and an alternative hypothesis \(H_1\). The null hypothesis states that there is no significant difference between the groups, while the alternative hypothesis states that there is a significant difference. We then define a suitable test statistic \(Z\)

text:
4.1 Cohort description

title: 5  Replicability study
text:
5.1 Across cycles
We have generated three “one-cycle” videos, corresponding to three cardiac pulsation. We compare in Figure 5.1 the \(\Delta CT\) obtained through three different methods: 1. We compute the optical flow along the CSI from the first frame to each other. We project the displacement along the CSI normal vector, and average these projections along the CSI. This gives us a \(\Delta CT\) for each frame, which we can plot as a function of time. 2. We take the segmentation mask, and for each A-scan, we fit a sinuodal function to its thickness. A-Scan that follows that pattern are kept, and the others are discarded. We then average the thickness of the remaining sinusoidal amplitudes. 3. We compute the thickness of the choroidal mask and simply takes its average per B-scan. \(\Delta CT\) is then computed as the difference between the maximum and minimum thicknesses along the cardiac cycle.

title: 6  How much the measured pulsability depends on an accurate detection of the heart rate?
text:
6.1 Which method is the most replicable?
Detecting the heart rate is a crucial step. Currently, it is chosen for two steps: selecting the best trace and demodulating the trace. We unfortunately only proxies to precisely estimate if we found the right heart rate or not. We can however test how much the measured pulsability depends on the heart rate detection by comparing the pulsability measured with the imposed heart rate and the demodulated heart rate.
Our experimental setup is as follow:
We can write this as: \[
  \delta CT(\text{imposed BPM}) = \delta CT(\text{detected BPM} \cdot \epsilon)
  \]
We vary \(\epsilon\) from increment ranging from 0.9 to 1.1, and we measure the pulsability for each cycle. We can then compare the pulsability measured with the imposed heart rate and the demodulated heart rate.
The first question we ask is similar to the reproducibility analysis: which method is the most replicable? We can compute the Pearson correlation between cycle 0 and cycle 1, and cycle 1 and cycle 2, for each video, for the imposed bpm and the id_demod bpm. This is shown in the Figure 6.1.
Fortunately, the results are promising: the correlation is the highest for the demodulated signal, and the lowest for the imposed bpm. This means that the demodulated signal is more replicable than the imposed bpm. The linear phase signal is in between, which is expected: it is a compromise between the two. Note: the imposed BPM case represents all the different heart rates that we imposed, over the same signal. Points are therefore not independant, and this does not represent which \(\epsilon\) is the worst.

title: 6  How much the measured pulsability depends on an accurate detection of the heart rate?
section: 6.2 Which method leads to the most pulsatile results?
text:
6.2 Which method leads to the most pulsatile results?
We know meaure which BPM leads to the largest \(\delta CT\). We can therefore compare the \(\delta CT\) measured with the demodulated signal and the imposed BPM. This is shown in Figure 6.2. The left panel shows the sensitivity curve for each video, with the median and interquartile range across videos. The right panel shows a paired comparison of the linear phase and demodulated \(\delta CT\) at the detected BPM. \(\delta CT\) is always normalized by the largest \(\delta CT\) measured for each video, to account for the fact that some videos are more pulsatile than others. The results are conclusive: the demodulated signal leads to the largest \(\delta CT\), and the imposed BPM leads to the smallest \(\delta CT\). The further the imposed BPM is from the detected BPM, the smaller the \(\delta CT\) is. This means that the demodulated signal is more pulsatile than the imposed bpm. The linear phase signal is in between, which is expected: it is a compromise between the two.









Figure 6.2: Peak analysis of the sensitivity curves. Left: sensitivity curve for each video, with the median and interquartile range across videos. Right: paired comparison of the linear phase and demodulated deltaCT at the detected BPM.

section: 6.3 How many videos reach their peak \(\delta CT\) outside of the detected BPM?
text:
6.3 How many videos reach their peak \(\delta CT\) outside of the detected BPM?
We now turn to quantifying how many videos reach their peak \(\delta CT\) outside of the detected BPM. This is shown in Figure 6.3. The left panel shows the distribution of the offset between the detected BPM and the BPM that leads to the largest \(\delta CT\). The right panel shows the cumulative distribution of the offset between the detected BPM and the BPM that leads to the largest \(\delta CT\). Once again, we reach a clear conclusion: 83% of the videos reach their peak at 3.3% or less from the detected BPM. This means that the detected BPM is a good proxy for the BPM that leads to the largest \(\delta CT\).

6.4 Does it matter if the detected BPM is correct or not?
Not finding the BPM will lead to a different \(\delta CT\). The question is: does it matter in the end? In others, not detecting the BPM could simply be caused by a low SNR, and the \(\delta CT\) measured could be small anyway. We can therefore compare the \(\delta CT\) measured with the demodulated signal and the imposed BPM, for videos that have a low SNR and videos that have a high SNR. This is shown in Figure 6.4.

title: 7  The anatomical pulsation
text:
7.1 Preliminary results
The core underlying argument of the ocular rigidity is that the inflation of the eye is driven by blood pulsation along a cardiac cycle, which manifests as a cyclic thickness variation of the choroid. However, there is a gap in the transition from the 2D estimation of thickness and its extension to a 3D volume change: we do not know if the pulsability is uniform across the entire sub-foveal choroid, or at least homogeneous enough to be considered as such. One hypothesis is that in contrary, it is driven by anatomical landmarks, such as the caliber of the choroidal vessels, and the angle of the slice with respect to the choroidal vasculature. In this chapter, we will explore the anatomical pulsation of the choroid, and its potential impact on the ocular rigidity.
As a preliminary result, I’ve inflicted myself with repeated measurements of my right eye during two days.
We can verify these results quantitatively: not only the thickness of the choroid is different between the three acquisitions, but there is vast differences in the pulsatile thickness, and the relative change of the choroid. The results are summarized in Figure 7.3.

7.1.1 3D Vessels Segmentation

7.1.1.1 Methods
The goal of this analysis is to locate the large choroidal vessels in 3D around the fovea, so that the B-scans used for the pulsation measurements can be related to the vessels they cross. We use the volume scan acquired on day 2 (6 × 6 mm angiography protocol, 503 B-scans of 500 A-scans, 1536 samples per A-scan). The device exports two co-registered channels: the structural OCT amplitude and the OCTA flow signal (decorrelation). The voxel size is 12.0 µm between A-scans, 11.9 µm between B-scans, and 1.95 µm axially.
Choroid segmentation. Each B-scan is segmented with the choroid segmentation model used throughout this work. The upper boundary of the mask is Bruch’s membrane (BM) and the lower one is the choroid–sclera interface (CSI). Both are extracted per A-scan.
Motion correction between B-scans. Unlike the repeated B-scans used for the pulsation measurements, every B-scan in a raster volume is acquired at a different position. The eye moves during the ~6 s acquisition, so neighbouring B-scans are displaced axially by amounts that do not correspond to anatomy. The BM jumps by up to ~85 px (~165 µm) over a few B-scans, which is incompatible with a 12 µm spacing between them. We estimate this motion from the BM and remove it:

For each B-scan \(t\), a line \(\text{BM}_t(x) = a_t + b_t\,(x - x_c)\) is fitted by least squares, where \(x_c\) is the central A-scan.
Along the slow (inferior–superior) axis, the anatomical component of \(a_t\) and \(b_t\) is modelled as a second-order polynomial, fitted robustly by iteratively reweighted least squares with Tukey’s biweight. This accounts for the curvature of the eye. The residuals \(\Delta a_t\) and \(\Delta b_t\) are taken as motion.
Every A-scan is shifted axially by \(\Delta a_t + \Delta b_t\,(x - x_c)\), using linear interpolation for the amplitude and flow volumes and nearest-neighbour interpolation for the choroid masks. Amplitude and flow receive the same shift, since they come from the same acquisition.

Before fitting, we flag corrupted B-scans. The mean amplitude in a slab below the BM is dominated by the shadows of the retinal vessels, which are continuous across a valid raster. A B-scan whose shadow profile correlates with neither neighbour, with the correlation more than 6 median absolute deviations below the median, is excluded from the fit and from the analysis. In this volume, this concerns only the last three B-scans. Lateral displacements between neighbouring B-scans, measured by cross-correlating the shadow profiles, were 0 ± 1 px, except for a single ~30 px jump, and were not corrected. The median axial jump of the BM between neighbouring B-scans went from 2.0 px before correction to 0.45 px after. Slow drift over the acquisition cannot be separated from the curvature of the eye with a single raster scan, so it remains in the anatomical component.
Vessel segmentation. Single B-scans are too noisy to segment the choroidal vessels reliably, for instance with a per-B-scan Niblack threshold. We therefore segment them in 3D, on the motion-corrected volume, combining both channels. In both, the lumen of the large vessels is dark.

Flattening and resampling. Both volumes are resampled so that the BM is a flat plane, keeping 330 samples (~640 µm) below it. The BM is first smoothed with a 3 × 9 median filter followed by a Gaussian filter (σ = 1 B-scan, 3 A-scans). The axial dimension is then averaged in bins of 6 samples, which gives nearly isotropic voxels (~12 µm) and reduces speckle. Voxels deeper than the smoothed choroidal thickness (CSI − BM, Gaussian σ = 2) are excluded.
Normalisation and fusion. Each channel is divided by its median over the A-scans of each B-scan at each depth. This removes both depth attenuation and B-scan-to-B-scan intensity changes. Each channel is then divided by a broad lateral background (Gaussian, σ = 30 voxels) and log-transformed, \(\log(I + 0.05)\), which turns the multiplicative speckle into additive noise. The two channels are standardised inside the choroid and averaged with equal weights.
Removal of retinal shadows. The retinal vessels cast thin shadows that are identical at every depth. We compute the lateral high-frequency detail of the fused volume (the volume minus its Gaussian-smoothed version, σ = 4 voxels), take its median over depth inside the choroid, and subtract it from every layer.
Tube enhancement. For each scale σ ∈ {3, 4.5, 6, 8} voxels (~35–100 µm; these scales respond best to vessels ~100–270 µm in diameter), we compute the eigenvalues of the scale-normalised Hessian (\(\sigma^2 H\)), sorted by magnitude \(|\lambda_1| \le |\lambda_2| \le |\lambda_3|\). A dark tube has \(\lambda_2, \lambda_3 > 0\) and \(\lambda_1 \approx 0\). The response is \[R_\sigma = \sqrt{\lambda_2 \lambda_3}\,\exp\!\left(-\frac{\lambda_1^2}{2\,(0.5\,\lambda_2)^2}\right) \quad \text{if } \lambda_2, \lambda_3 > 0, \text{ else } 0,\] and the vesselness \(R\) is its maximum over scales. The response is set to zero within two voxels of the BM and CSI, where the boundaries would otherwise appear as dark tubes. Because the thick subfoveal choroid gives a weaker response, \(R\) is normalised by its local level: \(R / (G_{40} * R + 0.5\,\overline{G_{40} * R})\), where \(G_{40}\) is a lateral Gaussian with σ = 40 voxels.
Thresholding. A voxel is labelled as vessel if (i) it belongs to a hysteresis segmentation of the normalised response, with the high and low thresholds set to its 95th and 85th percentiles inside the choroid, and (ii) it passes a 3D Niblack test on the fused signal smoothed with a Gaussian (σ = 2): \(F < m + k\,s\), with \(m\) and \(s\) the local mean and standard deviation over a 61 × 21 × 61 voxel window and \(k = -0.2\). Connected components smaller than 20 000 voxels (~0.03 mm³) are discarded. Together with the scales of the Hessian, this restricts the segmentation to the main choroidal vessels.

The segmentation was checked visually on B-scans and en-face slabs, but not against manual annotations. It likely under-segments the thick subfoveal choroid, where the signal is weakest.
Fovea and visualisation. The fovea is located at the minimum of the retinal thickness map (ILM to BM). The map is smoothed with a Gaussian (σ = 8 px), and a quadratic penalty on the distance to the centre of the scan is added before taking the minimum. The vessel surface is extracted by marching cubes from the vessel mask (smoothed with a Gaussian, σ = 1 voxel), and each vertex is mapped back to its depth below the BM. Figure 7.4 shows the vessels together with the BM and CSI surfaces, and two amplitude sections through the fovea along the temporal–nasal and inferior–superior axes.







Figure 7.4: Main choroidal vessels between the BM and the CSI after motion correction, with temporal–nasal and inferior–superior slices through the fovea. Vessel colour gives depth below the BM. The figure is interactive: drag to rotate, scroll to zoom, and click the legend to hide a surface.

title: 9  Correlation analysis
text:
9.1 Correlation analysis - Structural and biomechanical characteristics
In this section, we focus on establishing the correlation between each visit measurements (taken at the same time) and biomechanicals characteristics extracted from the data. Each point therefore represents a visit, and the correlation is computed across all visits. The correlation coefficient is computed using the Pearson method. Let’s first visualize what correlates with the intraocular pressure (IOP) measured.
We do not see a strong correlation between the intraocular pressure and the ocular rigidity, change in choroidal thickness or change in ocular volume. On the other hand, we have a pretty good correlation between the ocular pulse amplitude (OPA) and the change in choroidal thickness or change in ocular volume (Figure 9.2 ).
Let’s plot how the change in choroidal thickness correlates with the minimal choroidal thickness (Figure 9.3). The thicker the choroid, the more it can change in thickness.
We observe another mild correlation between the axial length and the change in choroidal thickness and the minimal choroidal thickness (Figure 9.4). This is fairly consistent with the literature: myopic eyes (longer axial length) tend to have thinner choroids (Meng et al. (2023))
Another potentially interesting correlation is between age and the choroidal thickness (previously documented (2025)-, approximately 12.7-15.6 μm per decade). In our cohort, we observe a stronger trend (around 25 μm per decade) between age and the change in choroidal thickness (Figure 9.5).

title: 10  Predictive analysis
text:
10.1 Slopes and follow-up
In Chapter 9, each point is a visit and both variables are measured at the same time. Here we take a variable at the first visit and correlate it with the slope of another variable over the follow-up, in unit per year. Each point is therefore an eye and not a visit. We have ?var:pred.n_eyes eyes, with ?var:pred.visits_min to ?var:pred.visits_max visits each and a median follow-up of ?var:pred.median_followup years.
Progression in glaucoma has no good predictor, and the IOP, which is what we treat, is a weak one. So we keep the IOP in every comparison below and read the other variables against it. The question is not whether a variable predicts progression well, it is whether it does better than what we already rely on.
A slope computed on two visits a few months apart is not progression. Figure 10.1 shows the ocular rigidity at the first visit against the MD slope, with all the eyes on the left, and only the eyes with at least ?var:pred.min_visits visits over at least ?var:pred.min_span year on the right. The trend on the left is carried by the eyes with the shortest follow-up.
The worst MD slope, at ?var:pred.worst_md_slope dB/year, comes from an eye with ?var:pred.worst_md_visits visits over ?var:pred.worst_md_span year (Figure 10.2).

10.2 Comparing the predictors
Figure 10.8 puts every baseline variable against the four endpoints, with the IOP in red.









Figure 10.3






The IOP is flat on the three structural endpoints and only moves on the MD slope, where it goes the wrong way: a higher pressure at the first visit goes with a slower MD loss. That is what we would expect if the eyes with the highest pressure are also the ones whose treatment was adjusted.
Against that, the ocular rigidity matches the IOP on the MD slope and in the direction we expect, a stiffer eye losing MD faster (Figure 10.4). It also tracks the PSD and the BMO-MRW slopes, where the IOP does nothing.
